#1 Hello,

I have been thinking about the differential cohomology diagram, which in standard applications seems to mostly be deployed as a static taxonomy (Given a gauge group G, we read off the associated moduli stack at the center and identify the surrounding nodes with known geometric objects).

But I’ve been working with a strong intuition that the hexagon possesses the capacity to act as a constructive engine based on discrete topological input, systematically generating continuous fields and discrete observable spectra. My thinking is that by taking the shape corner and traversing the Π-fracture square, we might be able to naturally lift to a physical state, and then project onto the flat moduli to extract holonomy.

Any direction on this is greatly appreciated, and I would be happy to expand on my thinking if at all helpful. Thank you for your time.

#2 Replying with a clarifying update, as I am hoping to get clarification myself. My reasoning can be found here: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20511582, but I will summarize in hopes someone here can enlighten me:

Instead of a cobordism functor evaluating directed types of quantum states, could one evaluate a directed tower of cohesive toposes, which constructs increasingly complex types of quantum systems, which themselves can be evaluated internally to each slice to yield local dynamics? The standard model might then result from slicing those groups (i.e. U(1)xSU(2)xSU(3)xSO(1,3)), and working within that specific slice topos in the tower?

The lack of literature evidence (requested in the title, and why I’m sharing a link to my writing instead of a nlab page) makes me suspect my intuition is wrong, so again any direction regarding this so that I may resolve my confusion is greatly appreciated.
